title: GUTs: The Unification of Forces
lead: Physicists search for one theory in which the four basic forces are different manifestations of a single force. This section describes electroweak theory, the gluons that carry the strong force and change the colors of quarks, the Standard Model that joins them, and the grand unified theories that would bring in the strong force, with the decay of the proton they predict.
objectives: Describe the principle of quantum chromodynamics.
summary_html:
• Attempts to show unification of the four forces are called Grand Unified Theories (GUTs) and have been partially successful, with connections proven between EM and weak forces in electroweak theory.
  • The strong force is carried by eight proposed particles called gluons, which are intimately connected to a quantum number called color—their governing theory is thus called quantum chromodynamics (QCD). Taken together, QCD and the electroweak theory are widely accepted as the Standard Model of particle physics.
  • Unification of the strong force is expected at such high energies that it cannot be directly tested, but it may have observable consequences in the as-yet unobserved decay of the proton and topics to be discussed in the next chapter. Although unification of forces is generally anticipated, much remains to be done to prove its validity.
notes: Three slips are carried as the book prints them: “transform the, and Z⁰” with the W⁺ and W⁻ missing, “the carriers of the weak and certainly of the electromagnetic force” where the strong force is meant, and the caption of Figure 33.25, which describes a Tevatron search for the Higgs boson while the photograph shows a proton decay detector.
exercise_notes: Bloom levels, concept tags and hints are AI-generated. Answers come from the book’s own key. Four unkeyed Integrated Concepts problems are left out (the γ rays from a neutral pion’s decay, the lifetime and range of a π⁺ made by 1.00-TeV protons, the lifetime and range of 500-MeV kaons, and the arrival of supernova neutrinos), as are the two Construct Your Own Problem items on a cosmic ray shower and on electron decay. The five conceptual questions carry AI-marked suggested approaches; two of them, on the evidence for electroweak unification and on whether gluons are confined, are printed with 33.5 and set here, where electroweak theory and gluons are introduced. The module prints no Check Your Understanding box, so nothing is set inline.

figures.original_caption: The exchange of a virtual Z⁰ carries the weak nuclear force between an electron and a neutrino in this Feynman diagram. The Z⁰ is one of the carrier particles for the weak nuclear force that has now been created in the laboratory with characteristics predicted by electroweak theory.

In figure (a), the eight types of gluons that carry the strong nuclear force are divided into a group of six that carry color and a group of two that do not. Figure (b) shows that the exchange of gluons between quarks carries the strong force and may change the color of a quark.
This Feynman diagram is the same interaction as shown in Figure 33.6, but it shows the quark and gluon details of the strong force interaction.

The relative strengths of the four basic forces vary with distance and, hence, energy is needed to probe small distances. At ordinary energies (a few eV or less), the forces differ greatly as indicated in Table 33.1. However, at energies available at accelerators, the weak and EM forces become identical, or unified. Unfortunately, the energies at which the strong and electroweak forces become the same are unreachable even in principle at any conceivable accelerator. The universe may provide a laboratory, and nature may show effects at ordinary energies that give us clues about the validity of this graph.

exercises.prompt: If a GUT is proven, and the four forces are unified, it will still be correct to say that the orbit of the moon is determined by the gravitational force. Explain why.

answer.solution: The forces become identical only at extremely high energies and small distances, near $10^{19}\;\text{GeV}$ for gravity. At the energies and distances of the Moon’s orbit they are as distinct as Table 33.1 shows: the strong and weak forces do not reach beyond a nucleus, and the Moon and the Earth are electrically neutral overall, so the electromagnetic attractions and repulsions of their charges cancel. Gravity is attractive only and has an infinite range, so it adds up over their enormous masses. A unified theory would show the four forces to be manifestations of one, but under these ordinary circumstances it is the gravitational manifestation that acts between the Moon and the Earth.

exercises.prompt: If the Higgs boson is discovered and found to have mass, will it be considered the ultimate carrier of the weak force? Explain your response.

answer.solution: No. The weak force is transmitted by the exchange of the $W^{+}$, $W^{-}$ and $Z^{0}$, as the photon transmits the electromagnetic force. The Higgs boson is the particle associated with the theory that the carrier particles are identical under certain circumstances; finding it would give that theory validity, explaining why the weak carriers are massive at ordinary energies, but it would not be the particle exchanged between the particles that feel the weak force. At the highest energies the weak carriers are expected to become massless, like photons and gluons, not to become the massive Higgs boson.

exercises.prompt: Gluons and the photon are massless. Does this imply that the $W^{+}$, $W^{-}$, and $Z^{0}$ are the ultimate carriers of the weak force?

answer.solution: Not necessarily. The $W^{+}$, $W^{-}$ and $Z^{0}$ are massive at ordinary energies, which is why the weak force has so short a range. But at higher energies their masses become less and less relevant and the $Z^{0}$ resembles the photon, and at still higher energies they are expected to transform into massless carriers more similar to photons and gluons. So the massive $W$ and $Z$ may be how the weak force’s carriers appear at ordinary energies, while a unified theory would make all the carriers massless and alike.

Electroweak theory predicted three carrier particles with spin 1, the $W^{+}$ and $W^{-}$ with masses of about $81\;\text{GeV}/c^{2}$ and the $Z^{0}$ with about $90\;\text{GeV}/c^{2}$, and in 1983 they were observed at CERN with those characteristics. Experiments show the strengths of the electromagnetic and weak forces becoming the same at energies of about 100 GeV, distances of about $10^{-18}\;\text{m}$. On a much larger scale, precise measurements of atomic energy levels and spectra show the weak force acting on electrons that spend time in the nucleus.

exercises.prompt: The quarks in a particle are confined, meaning individual quarks cannot be directly observed. Are gluons confined as well? Explain

answer.solution: Gluons carry color charge, six of them a color and an anticolor, so like quarks they may be confined to systems whose total color is white. They have not been directly observed: the evidence for them is indirect, from the momenta of the quarks in nucleons, which are smaller than they would be if there were no gluons to carry some of the momentum.

figure.alt: The figure shows an extremely energetic cosmic ray penetrating into the Earth’s atmosphere. High up in the atmosphere, the cosmic ray disintegrates into a shower of particles that start a chain reaction by themselves creating further particles. All these particles shower the surface of the Earth.
figure.caption: An extremely energetic cosmic ray creates a shower of particles on earth. The energy of these rare cosmic rays can approach a joule (about $10^{10}\;\text{GeV}$) and, after multiple collisions, huge numbers of particles are created from this energy. Cosmic ray showers have been observed to extend over many square kilometers.

exercises.prompt: The intensity of cosmic ray radiation decreases rapidly with increasing energy, but there are occasionally extremely energetic cosmic rays that create a shower of radiation from all the particles they create by striking a nucleus in the atmosphere as seen in the figure given below. Suppose a cosmic ray particle having an energy of $10^{10}\;\text{GeV}$ converts its energy into particles with masses averaging $200\;\text{MeV/}c^{2}$. (a) How many particles are created? (b) If the particles rain down on a $1.00\text{-km}^{2}$ area, how many particles are there per square meter?

parts.hint: Divide the cosmic ray’s energy by the rest energy of one particle, with both in the same unit.

exercises.prompt: What is the wavelength of a 50-GeV electron, which is produced at SLAC? This provides an idea of the limit to the detail it can probe.

answer.hint: At 50 GeV the electron’s rest energy is negligible, so its momentum is about $E/c$; then use $\lambda = h/p$.

exercises.prompt: The primary decay mode for the negative pion is $\pi^{-}\to \mu^{-}+\bar{\nu}_{\mu}$. (a) What is the energy release in MeV in this decay? (b) Using conservation of momentum, how much energy does each of the decay products receive, given the $\pi^{-}$ is at rest when it decays? You may assume the muon antineutrino is massless and has momentum $p=E/c$, just like a photon.

answer.solution: (a) 33.9 MeV (b) Muon antineutrino 29.8 MeV, muon 4.1 MeV (kinetic energy)

parts.hint: Subtract the muon’s rest energy from the pion’s, both from Table 33.2.
The two products leave with equal and opposite momenta, and their energies share the energy released.
The muon’s kinetic energy is what is left of the energy released.

exercises.prompt: Suppose you are designing a proton decay experiment and you can detect 50 percent of the proton decays in a tank of water. (a) How many kilograms of water would you need to see one decay per month, assuming a lifetime of $10^{31}\;\text{y}$? (b) How many cubic meters of water is this? (c) If the actual lifetime is $10^{33}\;\text{y}$, how long would you have to wait on an average to see a single proton decay?

parts.hint: Find how many protons must be watched for two decays a month, since half are detected, then count the protons in a kilogram of water.
A lifetime 100 times longer gives decays 100 times less often in the same tank.

exercises.prompt: (a) How much mass is converted to energy when a proton and antiproton annihilate each other? (b) How much energy is produced in the conversion above? (c) If energy were to produce a proton-antiproton pair, how much energy would this take? (d) What characteristic other than one being antimatter is different for a proton and an antiproton?

answer.solution: (a) $2(1.67\times 10^{-27}\;\text{kg}) = 3.34\times 10^{-27}\;\text{kg}$ (b) $3.34\times 10^{-27}(3.00\times 10^{8})^{2}\;\text{joules} = 3.01\times 10^{-10}\;\text{joules}$ (c) $3.01\times 10^{-10}\;\text{joules}$ (d) The proton has a positive charge, and the antiproton has a negative charge.

parts.hint: Both particles are converted, each with the proton’s mass.
Making the pair takes the energy their annihilation gives.
